why: Clumsy tool use causes errors like clicking the wrong label, and wastes time.
Clumsy clicking causes mistakes.
steps: Learn the tool's main shortcuts on day one.
Keep the guideline and a search tab open.
Keep a notes file of key rules.
Start and pause the tracker correctly.
Check each task saved before moving on.
examples: Number keys choose labels instead of a menu.
A 30-minute lunch with the tracker running.
Logged time must be real work.
A task didn't save before the internet dropped.
25 tabs open, the guideline is lost.
Keep 4 tabs: task, guideline, search, notes.
Keep only what you need open.
mistakes: Working on a phone when a laptop is required
levels: Fast and accurate with the tools.
cv: "Worked efficiently in rating and annotation platforms; tracked errors in Excel and Google Sheets."
This shows you can use the tools.
check: What should you do with the tracker on a break?
Pause it.
Name the four tabs to keep open.
Task, guideline, search and notes.
prac: Try free tools like Label Studio.
Practise spreadsheet sorting and filtering.
Learn your browser's tab shortcuts.

tasks.sit: A contributor draws boxes correctly but forgets to click Save before moving on.
tasks.ask: What happens if you don't save?
tasks.task: What happens, and what's the habit?
tasks.ans: The work may be lost or incomplete. Always confirm each task has saved and submitted.
tasks.why: The work can be lost, like writing an essay and closing it without saving. Always check it saved.
tasks.km: Keep your work so it isn't lost.

tasks.sit: A project requires a laptop, but a contributor tries to work on a phone.
tasks.ask: Why not use a phone if a laptop is required?
tasks.ans: The tool may not work properly, boxes may be imprecise, and it may break project rules. Use the required device.
tasks.why: The tool may not work well, labels may be inaccurate, and it can break the rules.
tasks.km: A machine like a laptop or phone.
tasks.simple: Use the device the project requires.

tasks.sit: A labelling tool lets you press 1 for "car" and 2 for "person".
tasks.ask: Why learn number keys?
tasks.ans: Keyboard shortcuts save time on every object without reducing accuracy.
tasks.why: Pressing one key is faster than clicking a menu, every single time.
tasks.km: A key that does something quickly.

tasks.sit: A contributor's browser isn't supported and the tool keeps freezing.
tasks.ask: What fixes a freezing tool?
tasks.ans: Switch to a supported browser (such as Chrome, Edge, or Safari if listed) before continuing.
tasks.why: Switch to a browser the project supports, like Chrome or Edge, if listed.
tasks.km: The app you use to visit websites.

tasks.sit: A time tracker is still running during a lunch break.
tasks.ask: What should happen to the tracker at lunch?
tasks.ans: The tracker should be paused whenever you stop working.
tasks.why: Pause it. Only real working time should be recorded.
tasks.km: Software that records your work time.
tasks.simple: Pause the tracker when you stop.

tasks.sit: A contributor keeps the guideline open in a separate tab.
tasks.ask: Why keep the rules open in a tab?
tasks.ans: Rules can be checked quickly without leaving the task, reducing errors and time.
tasks.why: You can check a rule in seconds without leaving the task.
tasks.km: A separate page in your browser.
tasks.simple: Keep the rules open beside you.

tasks.sit: The zoom function is never used during polygon tasks.
tasks.ask: What happens without zoom?
tasks.ans: Imprecise edges. Zooming in helps place polygon points accurately.
tasks.why: The shape edges will be rough and inaccurate.
tasks.km: Make the picture bigger on screen.

tasks.sit: A contributor tracks their errors in a simple spreadsheet with columns: date, task type, error, fix.
tasks.ask: Why track your own errors?
tasks.ans: It shows patterns in their mistakes so they can fix the most common ones.
tasks.why: You'll see which mistakes you make most, so you can fix them.

tasks.sit: The internet disconnects often during tasks.
tasks.ask: What if the internet keeps dropping?
tasks.ans: Improve the connection before working, and check that tasks saved after any disconnection.
tasks.why: Fix the connection first, and check tasks saved after any drop.

tasks.sit: A contributor accidentally assigns a label to the wrong box because two boxes overlap.
tasks.ask: How do you avoid labelling the wrong box?
tasks.ans: Select the correct object before labelling, and check the label list before submitting.
tasks.why: Click the right object first, then label, then check the label list.
tasks.simple: Select the right object before labelling.

tasks.sit: The tool has an "undo" shortcut (Ctrl+Z).
tasks.ask: When is undo useful?
tasks.ans: To reverse a mistaken point or box quickly instead of redrawing everything.
tasks.why: When you make a mistake, undo fixes it instantly.

tasks.sit: A contributor uses a spreadsheet filter to find all tasks marked "flagged".
tasks.ask: What is a filter?
tasks.ans: Filtering: showing only rows that meet a condition.
tasks.why: A spreadsheet tool that shows only rows you choose, like all "flagged" tasks.
tasks.km: Show only what you want to see.
tasks.simple: Filters show only what you need.

tasks.sit: A new project uses an unfamiliar interface.
tasks.ask: What do you do with a new tool?
tasks.task: What should you do before starting paid tasks?
tasks.ans: Read the tool guide or help page and practise any available sample tasks.
tasks.why: Read its help page and try any practice tasks before paid work.
tasks.km: What the software looks like and how you use it.
tasks.simple: Learn the tool before paid work.

tasks.sit: A contributor opens 25 browser tabs and loses the guideline tab.
tasks.ask: How many tabs should you keep?
tasks.ans: Keep a small, organised set of tabs: task, guideline, search, notes.
tasks.why: Just a few: task, guideline, search and notes.

tasks.sit: The tool's auto-snap feature changes polygon edges unexpectedly.
tasks.ask: What if auto-snap changes your edges?
tasks.ans: Check how the feature works, turn it off if the guideline allows, and review polygons before submitting.
tasks.why: Learn what it does, turn it off if allowed, and check shapes before submitting.
tasks.km: A feature that moves edges automatically.

tasks.sit: A contributor saves notes in a text file named "Project rules".
tasks.ask: What goes in a rules notes file?
tasks.ans: Key rules, common edge cases and their answers, and reviewer feedback to remember.
tasks.why: Key rules, tricky cases and answers, and feedback to remember.
tasks.simple: Keep notes of rules and feedback.

tasks.sit: A task requires uploading a short video, but the file is too large.
tasks.ask: The video is too big. What helps?
tasks.ans: Knowing how to check and reduce file size or format, following the project's instructions.
tasks.why: Knowing how to make the file smaller, following the project's instructions.
tasks.km: How much space a file takes.

tasks.sit: A contributor doesn't know how to check word count.
tasks.ask: How do you count words?
tasks.ans: Paste the text into a word processor or online counter, or use the tool's built-in counter if available.
tasks.why: Paste the text into a word counter or word processor.

tasks.sit: The tool shows a warning: "Box extends outside image."
tasks.ask: The tool warns you. What do you do?
tasks.ans: Fix the box so it stays within the image edges; don't ignore tool warnings.
tasks.why: Fix the problem. Warnings are there to stop mistakes.
tasks.km: A message that something is wrong.

tasks.sit: A contributor practises with CVAT (Computer Vision Annotation Tool) before applying.
tasks.ask: Why practise with free tools?
tasks.ans: Assessments often use real tools; practice builds speed and precision.
tasks.why: Tests often use real tools. Practice makes you faster and more accurate.
tasks.km: Do something again and again to get better.

analogy: Reliability is like being the friend people trust to keep a promise. Nobody checks on you, but you do what you said, honestly.
Do good, honest work even when nobody watches.
skills.def: Reliability and integrity mean doing steady, honest work on time without anyone watching, and never using forbidden shortcuts like AI tools or fake hours.
skills.s: Work well and honestly, even when nobody is watching.
words: Being honest and doing the right thing.
The time something must be finished.
fits: You work alone and remotely. Platforms give more work to people they trust.
Trust brings more work.
why: One dishonest act, like using a forbidden AI tool, can end your access forever.
One cheat can end everything.
steps: Use the same steps on every task.
Keep quality checks, even when busy.
Tell the team early about problems.
examples: A worker used a chatbot to write ratings when it was forbidden.
Learn shortcuts and keep a rules notes file.
You'll miss a deadline because of a power cut.
You made the same error on 30 tasks.
Report it and fix it if allowed.
cv: "Delivered consistent, high-quality work independently and to deadlines in a remote environment."
This shows you can be trusted.
check: Can you use AI tools when the project forbids them?
No.
You'll miss a deadline. What do you do?
Tell the team early.
prac: Work in focused blocks with short breaks.
Track your tasks per hour and your quality together.
Write a simple daily work plan.

tasks.sit: A contributor has a daily target of 40 tasks but only completes 30 with high quality.
tasks.ask: 30 good tasks or 40 rushed ones?
tasks.ans: Keep quality high and improve speed through routine and tool habits; don't rush to hit the number.
tasks.why: Keep quality high and get faster slowly with good habits. Rushing lowers your score.

tasks.sit: A contributor uses a chatbot to write ratings on a project that forbids AI tools.
tasks.ask: What happens if you secretly use a chatbot?
tasks.ans: Removal from the project or loss of access. It's a serious integrity violation.
tasks.why: You can be removed. It's cheating when it's forbidden.
tasks.simple: Using forbidden AI tools can end your access.

tasks.sit: A contributor logs 8 hours but only worked 6.
tasks.ask: Logging 8 hours when you worked 6?
tasks.ans: Time fraud: an integrity violation that can end access permanently.
tasks.why: That's lying about time. It can end your access.

tasks.sit: A power cut means you'll miss a deadline.
tasks.ask: What do you do about a deadline you'll miss?
tasks.ans: Tell the project team early, explain briefly, and ask for guidance.
tasks.why: Tell the team early and explain.
tasks.simple: Tell the team early about problems.

tasks.sit: A friend offers to do some of your tasks to help you catch up.
tasks.ask: Can a friend do your tasks?
tasks.ans: No. The work must be your own; sharing accounts or tasks breaks platform rules.
tasks.why: No. Your work must be your own.

tasks.sit: A contributor works four hours without a break and notices mistakes increasing.
tasks.ask: Four hours without a break: what happens?
tasks.ans: Work in focused blocks with short breaks to keep accuracy steady.
tasks.why: Mistakes increase. Work in blocks with short breaks.

tasks.sit: You're 20% behind target. Two options: skip fact-checks or learn tool shortcuts.
tasks.ask: Skip checks or learn shortcuts?
tasks.ans: Learn tool shortcuts. Skipping fact-checks lowers quality and can fail audits.
tasks.why: Learn shortcuts. Skipping checks lowers quality.
tasks.simple: Speed up honestly, never by skipping checks.

tasks.sit: A contributor uses a VPN to appear to be in another country for a restricted project.
tasks.ask: Is faking your location OK?
tasks.ans: Breaking location rules can lead to a ban. Only apply to projects open to your real location.
tasks.why: No. Using a VPN to pretend to be elsewhere can get you banned.
tasks.km: A tool that hides your real location.

tasks.sit: You finish a batch early.
tasks.ask: You finish early. What's a good use of time?
tasks.task: What reliable action could you take?
tasks.ans: Review a sample of your own work for errors before submitting, or ask whether more tasks are available.
tasks.why: Check your own work, or ask if more tasks are available.
tasks.simple: Use spare time to check your work.

tasks.sit: A contributor accepts more tasks than they can finish and abandons half.
tasks.ask: Why not grab more tasks than you can do?
tasks.ans: Abandoned tasks slow the project. Accept only what you can complete well.
tasks.why: Unfinished tasks slow the project. Take only what you can finish well.
tasks.simple: Only accept what you can finish.

tasks.sit: You realise you made the same labelling mistake on 30 tasks yesterday.
tasks.ask: You made the same mistake 30 times. What now?
tasks.ans: Report it honestly to the project team and fix the tasks if the platform allows; hiding it damages trust.
tasks.why: Tell the team and fix them if allowed. Hiding it breaks trust.

tasks.sit: A contributor writes "I don't know" in a rationale when they genuinely can't verify a claim.
tasks.ask: Is "I couldn't verify this" OK?
tasks.ans: Yes. It's better to say a claim couldn't be verified than to guess.
tasks.why: Yes. Being honest is better than guessing.

tasks.sit: A contributor sets a fixed start time and routine every day.
tasks.ask: Why a fixed routine?
tasks.ans: It builds steady output and makes deadlines predictable.
tasks.why: It keeps your work steady and on time.

tasks.sit: A task seems to take much longer than expected.
tasks.ask: A task is taking too long. What do you do?
tasks.ans: Follow the project's rules for long tasks (for example skip or flag), rather than rushing or silently exceeding limits.
tasks.why: Follow the project's rule for long tasks, like skipping or flagging.
tasks.simple: Follow the rules for long tasks.

tasks.sit: A contributor reads reviewer feedback only when scores drop.
tasks.ask: When should you read feedback?
tasks.ans: Read all feedback regularly, so small issues are fixed before they affect scores.
tasks.why: All the time, not only when scores drop.

tasks.sit: You're offered a proctored test and want to keep notes open "just in case".
tasks.ask: Can you keep notes open in a watched test?
tasks.ans: Close everything not allowed. Proctored tests check that the work is yours alone.
tasks.why: No. Close everything not allowed.
tasks.km: Watched and recorded during a test.

tasks.sit: A contributor tracks both tasks per hour and quality score each week.
tasks.ask: Why track speed AND quality?
tasks.ans: Speed alone can hide falling quality; tracking both keeps them balanced.
tasks.why: Speed alone can hide falling quality.

tasks.sit: A project ends suddenly.
tasks.ask: How do you prepare for a project ending?
tasks.ans: Save for quiet periods, keep your profile and CV updated, and maintain a good quality record for the next project.
tasks.why: Save money, keep your CV updated, and keep a good quality record.

tasks.sit: A contributor submits a task they know is unfinished to meet the target.
tasks.ask: Submitting unfinished work to hit the target?
tasks.ans: It hides poor work and fails audits. Finish properly or follow the rules for skipping.
tasks.why: It hides poor work and fails checks. Finish it or follow the skip rules.

tasks.sit: A contributor honestly reports a platform bug that let them see answer keys.
tasks.ask: Why report a bug that shows answers?
tasks.task: Why is this the right action?
tasks.ans: It protects the project's data and shows integrity, which builds long-term trust.
tasks.why: It protects the project and shows you're trustworthy.

analogy: A rubric is like the marking guide a teacher uses for an exam. Two teachers with the same guide should give the same mark.
Same guide, same mark.
skills.def: Rubric literacy means understanding exactly what each score in a rubric means, including its special rules and examples, and matching every answer to those written meanings.
skills.s: Know what each score means, and use those meanings every time.
words: A scoring guide with set levels.
One thing being scored, like accuracy.
A rule that sets the highest score allowed.
fits: The rubric is the LLM rater's main tool. Every score comes from it.
Every score comes from the rubric.
why: If raters read the rubric differently, their scores don't match, and the data is useless.
Different readings make useless data.
steps: Read every rubric line and its levels.
Learn the special rules, like caps.
Study the example answers for each level.
Match each answer to the closest written level.
When unsure, check examples, then flag.
goodbad: Can explain the difference between 3 and 4
Uses an old rubric from memory
examples: Rubric: 4 = minor issues only. One small typo.
Rule: any factual error caps Accuracy at 3. A great answer says Ghana uses the naira.
Accuracy is 3 at most. (Ghana uses the cedi.)
A wrong fact limits the score.
Rule: Safety is N/A if there is no risk. Prompt: a poem about rain.
Rule: don't punish length unless a limit was set. Long answer, no limit.
Don't lower any score for length.
levels: Knows the levels; misses special rules.
Applies every level and rule correctly.
cv: "Applied multi-criteria rubrics to evaluate AI responses."
This shows you understand scoring guides.
check: What is a cap?
A rule that limits the highest score.
Rubric: 4 = minor issues. One typo. Score?
prac: Rewrite each rubric level in your own words.
Score 5 sample answers and compare with examples.
Make a one-page rubric summary.

tasks.sit: A rubric says: 5 = no issues; 4 = minor issues only; 3 = at least one moderate issue; 2 = at least one major issue; 1 = unusable or unsafe. An answer has one small typo.
tasks.ask: Which score fits one typo?
tasks.ans: 4. A single typo is a minor issue, which matches the definition of 4.
tasks.why: The rubric says 4 = minor issues. A single typo is minor, so 4.
tasks.simple: Match the answer to the written level.

tasks.sit: Same rubric. An answer gives a wrong date for a deadline the user will act on.
tasks.ask: Is a wrong deadline small or big?
tasks.ans: Major. The user could miss the deadline, so it's a major accuracy issue; score 2 or lower.
tasks.why: Big (major). The user might miss the deadline because of it.
tasks.simple: Errors the user acts on are major.

tasks.sit: Same rubric. An answer contains dangerous advice.
tasks.ask: What score for dangerous advice?
tasks.ans: 1: the rubric defines 1 as unsafe.
tasks.why: 1. The rubric says 1 = unsafe.

tasks.sit: A rubric has five lines: Accuracy, Instruction following, Completeness, Clarity, Safety.
tasks.ask: How many scores for five lines?
tasks.task: How many separate scores do you give?
tasks.ans: Five, one for each line.
tasks.why: Five, one for each line.
tasks.simple: Each rubric line gets its own score.

tasks.sit: A rubric says "Completeness: does the answer address every part of the request?"
tasks.ask: What do you do before scoring completeness?
tasks.task: What must you do before scoring completeness?
tasks.ans: List every part of the request first, then check each one.
tasks.why: List every part of the question, then check each part was answered.

tasks.sit: A rubric note says: "Do not penalise length unless the user set a limit." An answer is long but the user set no limit.
tasks.ask: Should you lower a score for length?
tasks.task: Do you lower any score for length?
tasks.ans: No. The rubric note says length is only penalised when a limit was set.
tasks.why: No. The rubric note says only if the user set a limit.
tasks.km: An extra rule in the rubric.

tasks.sit: A rubric defines Clarity 3 as "understandable with effort".
tasks.ask: You had to reread twice. Which clarity score?
tasks.task: An answer is correct but badly organised; you had to reread it twice. What score?
tasks.ans: 3, because it was understandable only with effort, matching the definition.
tasks.why: 3, because the rubric says 3 = understandable with effort.
tasks.km: How easy something is to understand.
tasks.simple: Use the words in the definition.

tasks.sit: A rubric has an example answer scored 4 in the guideline.
tasks.ask: How do you use an example scored 4?
tasks.ans: Compare real answers with it to understand what a 4 looks like in practice.
tasks.why: Compare new answers with it to see what a 4 looks like.
tasks.km: A sample that shows the rule.
tasks.simple: Examples show what each score looks like.

tasks.sit: A rubric says "Any factual error caps Accuracy at 3." An answer has one minor factual error and is otherwise perfect.
tasks.ask: Highest accuracy with one wrong fact?
tasks.ans: 3. The cap rule sets the maximum regardless of other qualities.
tasks.why: 3. The cap rule says any factual error means 3 at most.
tasks.km: A limit on the highest score.
tasks.simple: Caps set the highest score allowed.

tasks.sit: A rubric uses Yes/No lines instead of numbers, such as "Follows the requested format: Yes/No".
tasks.ask: Yes or No for an extra heading?
tasks.task: The answer uses the right format but with one extra heading. Yes or No?
tasks.ans: Check the definition: if extra headings break the format, No; if the core format is met and the rubric allows extras, Yes. When unclear, follow examples or ask.
tasks.why: Check what counts as Yes. If unclear, look at examples or ask.
tasks.km: A rubric line with only two answers.

tasks.sit: A rubric line says "Safety: N/A if the topic has no safety risk."
tasks.ask: Safety score for a rain poem?
tasks.task: The prompt asks for a poem about rain. What do you mark?
tasks.ans: N/A, because there is no safety risk in the topic.
tasks.why: N/A. A poem about rain has no safety risk.
tasks.simple: Use N/A when the rubric allows it.

tasks.sit: The rubric is updated: Clarity moves from a 1 to 5 scale to a 1 to 3 scale.
tasks.ask: The scale changed. What now?
tasks.task: What do you need to do?
tasks.ans: Relearn the new definitions for 1, 2 and 3 and stop using the old 5-point meanings.
tasks.why: Learn the new 1 to 3 meanings and stop using the old ones.
tasks.simple: Relearn the rubric when it changes.

tasks.sit: A new rater gives 5 to everything that "looks good".
tasks.ask: What's wrong with giving 5 to everything that looks good?
tasks.ans: Rubric literacy: they're scoring by impression instead of matching each answer to the written definitions.
tasks.why: They're scoring by feeling, not by the rubric's written meanings.
tasks.km: Knowing exactly what each score means.
tasks.simple: Scores come from definitions, not feelings.

tasks.sit: A rubric says "Instruction following: all explicit instructions met = 5; one missed = 3; two or more missed = 1." An answer misses two instructions.
tasks.ask: Two instructions missed. What score?
tasks.why: 1. The rubric says two or more missed = 1.
tasks.simple: Count the missed instructions and use the table.

tasks.sit: A rubric line reads "Helpfulness: would the user be satisfied?"
tasks.ask: What should you imagine for helpfulness?
tasks.ans: The real user's goal, and whether this answer fully meets it.
tasks.why: The real user: would they be happy with this answer?

tasks.sit: Two rubric lines seem to overlap: Accuracy and Completeness. An answer leaves out a key step.
tasks.ask: Missing step: accuracy or completeness?
tasks.ans: Completeness, because nothing stated was wrong; something was missing. Only lower Accuracy if something stated is false.
tasks.why: Completeness. Nothing said was wrong; something was missing.
tasks.simple: Missing is completeness; wrong is accuracy.

tasks.sit: A rubric says "Rate the final answer, not the reasoning." An answer reaches the right final answer with messy working.
tasks.ask: Score the final answer or the working?
tasks.ans: Score the final answer as correct, following the rubric's instruction.
tasks.why: The rubric says the final answer, so score that.
tasks.simple: Rate what the rubric says to rate.

tasks.sit: A rubric defines "major issue" with examples: wrong facts, unsafe advice, missing the main question.
tasks.ask: Wrong currency symbol: major or minor?
tasks.task: An answer uses the wrong currency symbol for a price the user asked about. Major or minor?
tasks.ans: Likely major if it changes the meaning of the price the user needs; check the examples and choose the closest match.
tasks.why: Probably major, if it changes the price the user needs. Compare with the rubric's examples.

tasks.sit: A rater keeps a one-page summary of the rubric beside the task.
tasks.ask: Why keep a rubric summary beside you?
tasks.ans: It keeps the definitions in front of them, so every score is matched to the same wording.
tasks.why: So every score uses the same wording.

tasks.sit: You are unsure whether an issue is minor or moderate, and the rubric gives no example.
tasks.ask: Unsure between minor and moderate?
tasks.ans: Choose the level whose definition fits best, note your reasoning, and ask for guidance if the case keeps recurring.
tasks.why: Choose the closest level, note why, and ask if it keeps happening.
tasks.simple: When unsure, pick the closest level and ask.

analogy: Checking instructions is like checking a shopping list. If your mum asked for 6 items and you bring 5, the shopping isn't done.
Check every item on the list.
skills.def: Instruction-following checks mean listing every instruction in the prompt, including hidden ones, and checking the answer against each one.
skills.s: List every instruction, then tick each one.
words: Something the user asked the AI to do.
Not said directly, but clearly expected.
Hidden rules the AI was given.
fits: Instruction following is on almost every rubric.
It's scored on almost every task.
why: An answer can be correct but still fail the user if it ignores what they asked.
Correct but ignoring the ask still fails.
steps: Tick each instruction in the answer.
Score based on how many were missed.
goodbad: Judges the answer as a whole
examples: "Explain this to a 10-year-old." The answer uses hard words without explaining them.
A user writes in Hausa. The AI answers in English.
Hidden instruction: reply in the user's language.
"Three bullets, simple words, no links." The answer meets all three.
mistakes: Lowering Accuracy for an instruction miss
levels: Catches every instruction, stated or hidden.
cv: "Checked AI responses against explicit and implicit user instructions."
This shows you check what users asked.
check: What is an implicit instruction?
One not said directly but clearly expected.
A user writes in French. What language should the answer use?
French.
prac: List all instructions in 10 prompts before reading answers.
Practise spotting hidden instructions.
Count words with a tool.

tasks.sit: Prompt: "Reply in exactly three bullet points." The answer has three bullets plus a closing sentence.
tasks.ask: Three bullets plus an extra sentence: OK?
tasks.ans: No. "Exactly three bullet points" leaves no room for extra content outside them, unless the rubric allows brief framing.
tasks.why: No. "Exactly three bullet points" means nothing extra.

tasks.sit: Prompt: "Use simple words a child would understand." The answer uses "photosynthesis" without explanation.
tasks.ask: Is "photosynthesis" a child's word?
tasks.ans: No. An unexplained technical word breaks the simple-words instruction.
tasks.why: No. Without explanation, it breaks the "simple words" rule.

tasks.sit: Prompt: "Answer in Hausa." The answer is in English.
tasks.ask: English when Hausa was asked?
tasks.ans: No. The language instruction was ignored.
tasks.why: No. The language instruction was ignored.
tasks.km: The language the user asked for.
tasks.simple: The language requested must be used.

tasks.sit: Prompt: "Don't include any links." The answer ends with a website link.
tasks.ask: A link when "no links" was asked?
tasks.ans: An instruction violation: the answer includes a link.
tasks.why: It breaks the instruction. Mark it.

tasks.sit: Prompt: "Give me a title and a two-sentence summary." The answer gives a summary but no title.
tasks.ask: Title and summary asked; title missing?
tasks.ans: The title.
tasks.why: The title is missing. Mark it.

tasks.sit: Prompt: "List the steps in order." The steps are correct but step 3 should come before step 2.
tasks.ask: Steps correct but in the wrong order?
tasks.ans: No. The order instruction is broken even though the steps are correct.
tasks.why: No. Order was part of the instruction.

tasks.sit: Prompt: "Write it as a formal letter." The answer is a casual text message.
tasks.ask: Casual text instead of a formal letter?
tasks.ans: The format and tone instruction: a formal letter was requested.
tasks.why: The format and tone instruction failed.

tasks.sit: Prompt: "In under 100 words, explain what a budget is." The answer is 96 words.
tasks.ask: 96 words when under 100 was asked?
tasks.ans: Yes. 96 is under 100.
tasks.why: Yes, it meets the limit.

tasks.sit: System instruction: "Always end with a question to the user." The answer doesn't end with a question.
tasks.ask: No question at the end, against the system rule?
tasks.ans: An instruction-following failure against the system instruction.
tasks.why: Mark an instruction failure. System rules count too.
tasks.km: A hidden rule given to the AI.

tasks.sit: Prompt: "Explain this like I'm a beginner, not an expert." The answer uses expert words throughout.
tasks.ask: Expert words for a beginner?
tasks.ans: No: the audience level was ignored. Mark instruction following down.
tasks.why: No. The beginner level was ignored.
tasks.simple: Match the level of the reader.

tasks.sit: Prompt: "Give two options and recommend one." The answer gives two options but no recommendation.
tasks.ask: Two options, no recommendation?
tasks.ans: The recommendation.
tasks.why: The recommendation is missing.
tasks.simple: Check every verb in the prompt.

tasks.sit: Prompt: "Use a table with columns Name and Price." The table has columns Item and Cost.
tasks.ask: Different column names: a failure?
tasks.ans: A minor one: the structure is right but the column names differ from the request. Score according to the rubric's strictness.
tasks.why: A small one: the table is there but the names differ. Score by the rubric.
tasks.km: A vertical part of a table.
tasks.simple: Check the exact details asked for.

tasks.sit: Prompt: "Summarise without adding your opinion." The answer ends: "I think this is a great article."
tasks.ask: Opinion added when told not to?
tasks.ans: The no-opinion instruction.
tasks.why: The "without your opinion" rule failed.

tasks.sit: Prompt: "Rewrite this sentence in the past tense." The answer rewrites it in the future tense.
tasks.ask: Future tense when past was asked?
tasks.ans: No, the tense is wrong.
tasks.why: No, the tense is wrong.

tasks.sit: Prompt has two instructions that conflict: "Be detailed" and "Keep it under 20 words".
tasks.ask: Detailed AND under 20 words?
tasks.ans: Check the guideline for priority; many rubrics treat explicit numeric limits as stronger. Judge whether the answer handled the conflict sensibly and note it.
tasks.why: Check the rulebook for which wins; usually the number limit. Judge how well the answer balanced it.
tasks.simple: When instructions clash, follow the guideline's priority.

tasks.sit: Prompt: "Answer only yes or no." The answer says: "Yes."
tasks.ask: "Yes." when asked for yes or no?
tasks.ans: Yes.
tasks.why: Yes, it's correct.
tasks.km: A question answered with yes or no.
tasks.simple: Sometimes the shortest answer is correct.

tasks.sit: Prompt: "Include at least one example." The answer includes none.
tasks.ask: No example when one was asked?
tasks.ans: Instruction violation: no example was given.
tasks.why: Mark an instruction failure.
tasks.km: A sample that shows an idea.
tasks.simple: "At least one" means one or more.

tasks.sit: Prompt: "Use British spelling." The answer uses "centre" but also "color".
tasks.ask: "centre" but also "color"?
tasks.ans: A partial failure: one American spelling breaks the British spelling instruction.
tasks.why: Partly failed: one American spelling breaks the British rule.

tasks.sit: Prompt: "Don't mention prices." The answer says "affordable" but gives no numbers.
tasks.ask: Is "affordable" a price?
tasks.ans: Usually not: it's a description, not a price. Check the guideline if the project defines "price" more broadly.
tasks.why: Usually not. It describes, but gives no number. Check the rulebook if unsure.
tasks.simple: Check what the instruction really covers.

tasks.sit: An answer follows every instruction perfectly but is factually wrong.
tasks.ask: Perfect instructions, wrong fact: instruction score?
tasks.ans: High. Instruction following is scored separately; the error lowers Accuracy instead.
tasks.why: High. The wrong fact lowers Accuracy, not Instruction following.
tasks.km: Each line scored on its own.
tasks.simple: Following rules and being right are scored apart.

analogy: Accuracy checking is like checking a maths test. You don't just look at the final answer; you redo the sums yourself.
Redo the work yourself.
skills.def: Accuracy checking means confirming that every fact, number and calculation in an answer is correct, by recalculating and checking trusted sources.
skills.s: Make sure every fact and number is right.
fits: Accuracy is usually the most important rubric line.
It's often the most important score.
why: People act on AI answers. A wrong price or date can cost them.
People act on wrong answers.
steps: Split the answer into separate claims.
examples: Check which country a fact belongs to.
cv: "Verified factual accuracy and calculations in AI responses."
This shows you check facts and maths.
check: What should you do with the AI's maths?
Redo it yourself.
prac: Check every fact in 5 AI answers.
Redo 10 simple calculations from AI answers.
Learn trusted sources for common topics.

tasks.sit: An answer says the boiling point of water at sea level is 100°C.
tasks.ask: Does water boil at 100°C at sea level?
tasks.ans: Yes.
tasks.why: Yes, that's correct.
tasks.km: The temperature where a liquid boils.

tasks.sit: An answer says 1 hour has 3,600 seconds.
tasks.ask: Does an hour have 3,600 seconds?
tasks.why: Yes: 60 minutes × 60 seconds = 3,600.

tasks.sit: An answer says Nigeria has 36 states plus the Federal Capital Territory.
tasks.ask: Does Nigeria have 36 states plus the FCT?
tasks.ans: Yes.
tasks.why: Yes, that's correct.
tasks.km: Federal Capital Territory, where Abuja is.

tasks.sit: An answer says a triangle's angles add up to 360°.
tasks.ask: Do a triangle's angles add up to 360°?
tasks.ans: No. They add up to 180°.
tasks.why: No. They add up to 180°.
tasks.km: The space between two lines that meet.

tasks.sit: An answer says Ghana's currency is the naira.
tasks.ask: Is Ghana's money the naira?
tasks.ans: No. Ghana uses the cedi; the naira is Nigeria's.
tasks.why: No. Ghana uses the cedi. The naira is Nigeria's.
tasks.simple: Check which country a fact belongs to.

tasks.sit: An answer says 15% of 200 is 30.
tasks.ask: Is 15% of 200 equal to 30?

tasks.sit: An answer says the telephone was invented by Alexander Graham Bell, who got a patent in 1876.
tasks.ask: Who invented the telephone?
tasks.ans: Yes, that is the widely accepted record.
tasks.why: Bell is widely credited, with an 1876 patent.
tasks.km: Legal proof that you invented something.

tasks.sit: An answer says the Sun orbits the Earth.
tasks.ask: Does the Sun go around the Earth?
tasks.ans: No. The Earth orbits the Sun.
tasks.why: No. The Earth goes around the Sun.

tasks.sit: An answer says a kilogram is heavier than a pound.
tasks.ask: Is a kilogram heavier than a pound?
tasks.ans: Yes. 1 kg is about 2.2 pounds.
tasks.why: Yes. 1 kg is about 2.2 pounds.

tasks.sit: An answer says WhatsApp was created by Google.
tasks.ask: Did Google create WhatsApp?
tasks.ans: No. WhatsApp was founded by Jan Koum and Brian Acton and is owned by Meta.
tasks.why: No. Jan Koum and Brian Acton founded it; Meta owns it now.
tasks.km: The person who started a company.

tasks.sit: An answer says Lake Victoria is Africa's largest lake.
tasks.ask: Is Lake Victoria Africa's biggest lake?
tasks.ans: Yes, by surface area.
tasks.why: Yes, by surface area.
tasks.km: How much space the top covers.
tasks.simple: Some facts depend on how you measure.

tasks.sit: An answer says there are 12 months in a year and 53 weeks in every year.
tasks.ask: Does every year have 53 weeks?
tasks.ans: Partly: 12 months is right, but a year has 52 weeks and one or two extra days, not 53 full weeks.
tasks.why: No. A year has 52 weeks plus one or two days.

tasks.sit: An answer about a recipe says to bake bread at 50°C.
tasks.ask: Can you bake bread at 50°C?
tasks.ans: No. Bread is usually baked around 180 to 230°C; 50°C would not bake it.
tasks.why: No. Bread is usually baked around 180 to 230°C.

tasks.sit: An answer says a spider has six legs.
tasks.ask: Does a spider have six legs?
tasks.ans: No. Spiders have eight legs.
tasks.why: No. Spiders have eight legs. (Insects have six.)
tasks.km: A small animal with six legs.

tasks.sit: An answer says "Mount Kilimanjaro is about 5,895 metres high."
tasks.ask: Is Kilimanjaro about 5,895 metres high?
tasks.ans: Yes, that is the commonly cited height.
tasks.why: Yes, that is the usual figure.

tasks.sit: An answer's facts are all correct, but it states an opinion as a fact: "Jollof rice is the best food in the world."
tasks.ask: "Jollof is the best food in the world": fact or opinion?
tasks.ans: Note it as an opinion presented as fact; it isn't a factual error, but it may lower accuracy or neutrality depending on the rubric.
tasks.why: Opinion. It isn't a wrong fact, but it shouldn't be stated as fact.
tasks.km: What someone thinks, not a fact.

tasks.sit: An answer gives the correct formula for the area of a circle: πr².
tasks.ask: Is the area of a circle πr²?
tasks.ans: Yes.
tasks.why: Yes, correct.
tasks.km: A rule written with maths symbols.

tasks.sit: An answer says the Sahara Desert is in South America.
tasks.ask: Is the Sahara in South America?
tasks.ans: No. The Sahara is in northern Africa.
tasks.why: No. It's in northern Africa.
tasks.km: A very large area of land, like Africa.

tasks.sit: An answer says Africa has 54 recognised countries.
tasks.ask: Does Africa have 54 countries?
tasks.ans: Yes, 54 is the widely used count of UN-recognised African countries.
tasks.why: Yes, 54 is the widely used count.

tasks.sit: An answer says the speed limit on all roads worldwide is 100 km/h.
tasks.ask: Same speed limit everywhere?
tasks.ans: No. Speed limits differ by country and road type.
tasks.why: No. Limits differ by country and road. Watch out for "all" and "always".
tasks.km: Saying something is true for everything.
tasks.simple: Watch for claims that say "all" or "always".

analogy: A hallucination is like a person who confidently gives you directions to a shop that doesn't exist. They sound sure, but the shop isn't there.
Sounding sure doesn't make it real.
skills.def: Hallucination detection means spotting things the AI has made up, like fake sources, people, laws, numbers or events, especially when they sound confident and exact.
skills.s: Find things the AI made up.
words: Something the AI invented and said as fact.
A reference to a source, like a book or study.
fits: Hallucinations are a special kind of accuracy error that raters are hired to catch.
Catching made-up facts is a key job.
why: Made-up sources and numbers fool people because they look real.
Fake facts look real.
steps: Notice exact details with no source.
Try to find every cited source.
Search the exact name, title or number.
If nothing exists, flag it as fabricated.
Reward answers that honestly say "I don't know".
examples: "(Okeke & Bello, 2021, Journal of West African Learning)"
Search title, authors and journal: nothing.
Can't find it? It's probably fake.
Search official law sites: no such act.
User asks about a book that doesn't exist; the AI summarises it.
The AI should say it can't find the book.
Good AI says when something doesn't exist.
User asks about a fake book; AI says "I can't find that title."
levels: Checks every source and flags fakes.
cv: "Identified hallucinated facts, fabricated citations and unsupported claims."
This shows you catch made-up facts.
check: You can't find a cited study anywhere. What is it likely to be?
A fabricated (made-up) citation.
Is "I'm not sure" ever a good answer?
Yes, when the AI truly doesn't know.
prac: Ask an AI for sources on a small topic and check each one.
Practise searching exact titles in quotes.
Keep a list of hallucination warning signs.

tasks.sit: An answer cites "Adeyemi, T. (2019). Rice Farming in Kano. Lagos University Press" for a statistic. You can't find the book anywhere.
tasks.ask: Can you find the book?
tasks.ans: A possibly fabricated citation. Say you couldn't locate it and treat the statistic as unsupported.
tasks.why: No, so it's likely made up. Flag it and say you couldn't find it.
tasks.simple: If you can't find a source, flag it.

tasks.sit: An answer says a Nigerian law "Section 45(3) of the Digital Farming Act 2018" requires something. No such act can be found.
tasks.ask: Does the law exist?
tasks.task: What is this likely to be?
tasks.ans: A hallucinated law. Invented legal references are a serious accuracy problem.
tasks.why: No such act can be found, so it's likely invented.

tasks.sit: An answer quotes a famous person with no source, and the quote only appears on social media image sites.
tasks.ask: A quote only on social media pictures?
tasks.ans: As unverified and possibly fabricated. Mark it and note the lack of a reliable source.
tasks.why: Treat it as unverified, maybe fake.

tasks.sit: An answer gives a precise statistic: "73.4% of Nigerian students own laptops." No source is given.
tasks.ask: 73.4% with no source?
tasks.ans: Whether any reliable survey reports this figure. Precise numbers with no source are a common hallucination pattern.
tasks.why: Check for a reliable survey. Exact numbers without sources are often made up.

tasks.sit: An answer describes a feature of a phone model that doesn't exist.
tasks.ask: A phone feature that doesn't exist?
tasks.task: What kind of error is this?
tasks.ans: A hallucination: an invented product feature.
tasks.why: A hallucination: the AI invented it.

tasks.sit: An answer invents a website link that returns "page not found".
tasks.ask: A link that says "page not found"?
tasks.ans: A fabricated or broken link; note it in the rationale.
tasks.why: Mark it as a fake or broken link.
tasks.km: A web address that doesn't work.

tasks.sit: An answer says a real author wrote a book they never wrote.
tasks.ask: Did that author write that book?
tasks.ans: Search the book title with the author's name in a library catalogue or publisher site.
tasks.why: Search the title and author in a library or publisher website.
tasks.simple: Check who really wrote a book.

tasks.sit: An answer summarises a news event that you can't find in any news source.
tasks.ask: A news event no news site has?
tasks.ans: Treat it as unverified and likely invented; don't accept it without a reliable source.
tasks.why: It's probably invented. Don't accept it.
tasks.simple: Real events leave real news reports.

tasks.sit: An answer mixes a real study with a fake result: the study exists, but it never found what the answer claims.
tasks.ask: Real study, fake result?
tasks.ans: Misrepresentation of a real source: the citation is real, but the claim is not supported by it.
tasks.why: Flag it: the study exists, but it doesn't say that.
tasks.simple: A real source can still be misquoted.

tasks.sit: An answer confidently gives the phone number of a local bank branch. You can't verify it.
tasks.ask: A bank branch number you can't check?
tasks.ans: A made-up number could send users to the wrong place, or to a scammer. Flag it as unverified.
tasks.why: It could send people to the wrong place, or to a scammer. Flag it.
tasks.km: A person who tricks people out of money.

tasks.sit: An answer invents a historical date for a real event.
tasks.ask: A wrong date for a real event?
tasks.ans: Check the event date in a reliable encyclopedia or official record.
tasks.why: Check a trusted encyclopedia or official record.
tasks.km: A trusted book or site of facts.

tasks.sit: An answer says "According to the Central Bank of Nigeria" but gives a rule you can't find on the bank's website.
tasks.ask: The named source doesn't say it?
tasks.ans: Check the official website. If the rule isn't there, mark it as misattributed.
tasks.why: Mark it as misattributed: given to the wrong source.
tasks.km: Said to come from the wrong place.
tasks.simple: Check that the named source really says it.

tasks.sit: The user asks about a made-up book title. The AI writes a detailed summary of it.
tasks.ask: The AI summarised a fake book. What's wrong?
tasks.ans: A hallucination: the AI should have said it couldn't find the book instead of inventing a summary.
tasks.why: It should have said it couldn't find the book.
tasks.simple: Good AI says when something doesn't exist.

tasks.sit: The user asks about a made-up book. The AI says: "I can't find a book with that title. Could you check the author?"
tasks.ask: The AI said it can't find the book. Good?
tasks.ans: Yes. This is the honest behaviour you want to reward.
tasks.why: Yes. That's honest and should get credit.

tasks.sit: An answer gives an exact population figure for a small village.
tasks.ask: An exact population for a tiny village?
tasks.ans: Very. Specific figures for small places are rarely available and often invented; verify or mark as unsupported.
tasks.why: Be careful. Small places rarely have exact public numbers.
tasks.simple: Very specific facts about small places are risky.

tasks.sit: An answer names a "Professor Musa Bello of Harvard" as an expert. You can't find him.
tasks.ask: A professor you can't find?
tasks.ans: A possibly invented person or credential.
tasks.why: Flag a possibly invented person.

tasks.sit: An answer includes a recipe "from Chef Ada's award-winning book" with no trace online.
tasks.ask: "Chef Ada's book" you can't find?
tasks.task: How do you treat the attribution?
tasks.ans: As unverified; the recipe may be fine, but the attribution may be invented.
tasks.why: The recipe may be fine, but the book may be invented.

tasks.sit: An answer invents an extra step in a real process, such as a form that isn't needed to renew a passport.
tasks.ask: An extra step in a real process?
tasks.ans: Compare with the official process on the government website.
tasks.why: Compare with the official website.

tasks.sit: An answer's facts are correct, but it says "studies show" with no studies named.
tasks.ask: "Studies show" with no studies named?
tasks.ans: Not necessarily, but it's an unsupported claim. Ask whether the claim itself is true, and note the vague sourcing.
tasks.why: Not always made up, but weak. Check if the claim is true.

tasks.sit: You're unsure whether a fact is invented and have no time to check fully.
tasks.ask: No time to check fully?
tasks.ans: That you couldn't verify it, rather than guessing it's true or false.
tasks.why: Say you couldn't verify it. Don't guess.

analogy: Scoring separately is like a school report card. A bad maths mark doesn't lower your English mark.
Each subject gets its own mark.
skills.def: Scoring each criterion separately means giving every rubric line its own score, based only on problems that belong to that line.
skills.s: Each rubric line gets its own score.
words: A general feeling about the whole answer.
fits: AI teams use each line's score to fix a specific problem.
Each score shows a different problem.
why: If one problem lowers every line, nobody knows what really went wrong.
Mixed scores hide the real problem.
steps: Decide which rubric line it belongs to.
Match each problem to a line.
Leave the other lines alone if they're fine.
examples: Tone goes down; Accuracy stays high.
Each problem affects its own line.
Friendly, neat answer with a wrong date.
Accuracy goes down; Tone stays high.
Nice style doesn't hide wrong facts.
Perfect answer, 30 words over the limit.
Over the limit lowers only one score.
Answer with wrong format and two wrong facts.
mistakes: Letting one big problem lower everything
Choose one line unless told otherwise.
cv: "Scored AI responses independently across multiple quality dimensions."
This shows careful scoring.
check: Correct answer, rude tone. Which score goes down?
Tone.
Should a format mistake lower Accuracy?
No.
prac: For 5 answers, list problems and their lines before scoring.
Practise with answers that are right but rude.
Check your scores aren't all the same.

tasks.sit: An answer is accurate but rude.
tasks.ask: Which score goes down for rudeness?
tasks.ans: Tone goes down; Accuracy stays high.
tasks.why: Only Tone. The facts are still right, so Accuracy stays high.
tasks.km: How words feel to the reader.
tasks.simple: Each problem affects its own line.

tasks.sit: An answer is friendly and well formatted but has a wrong fact.
tasks.ask: Which score goes down for a wrong fact?
tasks.ans: Accuracy goes down; Tone and Clarity can stay high.
tasks.why: Only Accuracy. Being friendly doesn't make a wrong fact right.
tasks.simple: Don't let good style hide a wrong fact.

tasks.sit: An answer answers only one of two questions, correctly.
tasks.ask: One question answered out of two?
tasks.ans: Completeness goes down; Accuracy stays high for what was said.
tasks.why: Completeness goes down. What was said can still be accurate.

tasks.sit: An answer is correct but written as one huge paragraph.
tasks.ask: One giant paragraph?
tasks.ans: Clarity goes down; Accuracy stays high.
tasks.why: Clarity goes down. Facts stay fine.
tasks.km: How easy it is to read.
tasks.simple: Hard to read is a clarity problem.

tasks.sit: An answer follows all instructions but gives unsafe advice.
tasks.ask: All instructions followed, but unsafe?
tasks.ans: Safety (and likely Accuracy) goes down; Instruction following can stay high.
tasks.why: Safety goes down. Following instructions doesn't make it safe.
tasks.simple: Following instructions doesn't make it safe.

tasks.sit: An answer is 30 words over the limit but otherwise perfect.
tasks.ask: 30 words too long?
tasks.ans: Instruction following only.
tasks.why: Only Instruction following goes down.

tasks.sit: A rater gives an answer 2 on every line because it had one serious error.
tasks.ask: One error, 2 on every line?
tasks.ans: They let one problem drag down unrelated lines. Only the affected lines should drop.
tasks.why: Wrong. One problem should only lower its own line.
tasks.simple: Don't punish every line for one problem.

tasks.sit: A rater gives 5 on every line because the answer "felt great".
tasks.ask: 5 everywhere because it felt great?
tasks.ans: They scored by overall impression, not line by line.
tasks.why: Wrong. Check each line against its definition.
tasks.simple: Check each line on its own.

tasks.sit: An answer uses the wrong format and has two factual errors.
tasks.ask: Wrong format and two wrong facts?
tasks.ans: Instruction following (format) and Accuracy both go down.
tasks.why: Two lines go down: Instruction following and Accuracy.

tasks.sit: An answer is correct and complete but ignores the requested British spelling.
tasks.ask: Ignored British spelling?
tasks.ans: Instruction following (or a style line if the rubric has one).
tasks.why: Instruction following (or a style line) goes down.

tasks.sit: An answer gives correct advice in a cold tone to a worried user.
tasks.ask: Correct advice, cold tone to a worried user?
tasks.ans: Tone or Helpfulness, depending on the rubric; Accuracy stays high.
tasks.why: Tone or Helpfulness goes down; Accuracy stays high.

tasks.sit: An answer invents a source for a true claim.
tasks.ask: A fake source for a true claim?
tasks.ans: Accuracy or Groundedness (for the fake source); the claim itself is true, so note that too.
tasks.why: Accuracy or Groundedness goes down for the fake source.
tasks.km: How well claims are backed by real sources.
tasks.simple: A fake source is its own problem.

tasks.sit: An answer is safe, correct and complete but very long for a simple question.
tasks.ask: Very long but perfect for a simple question?
tasks.ans: Conciseness or Helpfulness, if the rubric has one; otherwise it may not change any line.
tasks.why: Conciseness, only if the rubric has that line.
tasks.simple: Only score length if the rubric does.

tasks.sit: An answer's reasoning has a wrong step but the final answer is right. The rubric has Final Answer and Reasoning lines.
tasks.ask: Right answer, wrong step?
tasks.ans: Final Answer high, Reasoning lower.
tasks.why: Final Answer high, Reasoning lower.
tasks.simple: Right answer, wrong working: two separate scores.

tasks.sit: An answer refuses a harmless request politely.
tasks.ask: A polite refusal of a harmless request?
tasks.ans: Helpfulness (and possibly Instruction following) go down; Tone may stay high.
tasks.why: Helpfulness goes down. Tone can stay high.
tasks.simple: Polite refusals of harmless requests still fail.

tasks.sit: You notice you always give the same score on every line.
tasks.ask: You give the same score everywhere. Why?
tasks.ans: You may be scoring by overall impression. Recheck each line against its own definition.
tasks.why: You may be scoring by feeling. Check each line on its own.
tasks.simple: Identical scores everywhere is a warning sign.

tasks.sit: An answer is perfect except for a missing example the user requested.
tasks.ask: Missing a requested example?
tasks.ans: Completeness or Instruction following, depending on the rubric's definitions.
tasks.why: Completeness or Instruction following, whichever the rubric says.
tasks.km: A sample that shows an idea.
tasks.simple: Find the line that matches the problem.

tasks.sit: Two lines both seem to fit one problem.
tasks.ask: One problem fits two lines?
tasks.ans: Check the rubric's definitions or examples to choose one line, so you don't count the problem twice unless the rubric says to.
tasks.why: Use the rubric's definitions to pick one, so you don't count it twice.
tasks.simple: Don't count one problem twice without reason.

tasks.sit: An answer has a spelling mistake in a heading.
tasks.ask: A spelling mistake in a heading?
tasks.ans: Clarity or Style, as a minor issue.
tasks.why: Clarity or style, as a small issue.

tasks.sit: An answer contains correct facts, a helpful tone, all instructions followed, and clear formatting.
tasks.ask: Everything perfect?
tasks.ans: Top scores on every line, with a specific rationale.
tasks.why: Top scores on every line, with a clear reason.

analogy: Helpfulness is like asking a shop assistant for help. A good one answers kindly and points you to the right shelf. A bad one is rude or sends you away.
Helpful and kind, not rude or useless.
skills.def: Tone and helpfulness judgment means deciding whether an answer meets what the user really needs in a way that feels respectful, warm when needed, and useful.
skills.s: Is it kind, and does it really help?
words: How much the answer helps the user.
Saying no to a harmless request.
Lecturing people when they didn't ask.
fits: Many rubrics have Tone or Helpfulness lines.
Tone and help have their own scores.
why: People stop using AI that is rude, preachy or unhelpful.
Rude or useless answers lose people.
steps: Ask: what does the user really need?
Check warmth if the user is upset.
Check for clutter: needless warnings or refusals.
examples: User failed a driving test. Answer starts "Obviously you weren't ready."
User asks how to remove a stain from a shirt. The AI refuses.
Simple pasta question; three paragraphs of warnings.
Too many warnings hide the answer.
mistakes: Ignoring tone because facts are right
levels: Spots subtle tone and helpfulness problems.
cv: "Assessed tone, helpfulness and user focus of AI responses."
This shows you care about the user.
check: The AI refuses to explain how to boil rice. Good or bad?
Bad: it's over-refusal.
Correct but rude: which score drops?
Tone.
prac: Rewrite 3 cold answers into warm ones.
Find needless warnings in AI answers.
Practise spotting preachy tone.

tasks.sit: A user writes: "I failed my exam again." The answer starts: "Here are study tips."
tasks.ask: What should come before study tips?
tasks.task: How could it be more helpful?
tasks.ans: Acknowledge the user's disappointment briefly and kindly before giving tips.
tasks.why: A short kind sentence about how disappointing it is.

tasks.sit: An answer says: "Obviously, you should have known this."
tasks.ask: What's wrong with "Obviously"?
tasks.ans: It's condescending.
tasks.why: It talks down to the user.

tasks.sit: An answer to "How do I cook beans?" includes three paragraphs of safety warnings.
tasks.ask: Too many warnings for cooking beans?
tasks.ans: Less helpful: unnecessary warnings bury the answer.
tasks.why: Less helpful. The warnings bury the answer.
tasks.km: Extra stuff that gets in the way.
tasks.simple: Too many warnings make answers worse.

tasks.sit: An answer to a business email request uses slang and emojis.
tasks.ask: Slang in a business email?
tasks.ans: The tone doesn't fit a professional context.
tasks.why: The tone doesn't fit a professional email.

tasks.sit: An answer says: "Great question! Here's the answer..." at the start of every reply.
tasks.ask: "Great question!" every time?
tasks.ans: Often a minor style issue: repetitive filler adds nothing. Score according to the rubric.
tasks.why: A small style issue: it adds nothing.

tasks.sit: An answer refuses: "I can't help with that" when asked how to remove a stain.
tasks.ask: Refusing to explain stain removal?
tasks.ans: Low: the request is harmless.
tasks.why: Low helpfulness. It's a harmless request.

tasks.sit: An answer gives correct information but no practical next step when the user asked what to do.
tasks.ask: No next step when asked what to do?
tasks.ans: Less helpful: the user wanted action steps.
tasks.why: Less helpful. The user wanted to know what to do.
tasks.simple: Give the user a way forward.

tasks.sit: A user asks for encouragement before an interview. The answer is a dry list of facts.
tasks.ask: Dry facts when encouragement was asked?
tasks.ans: Warmth and encouragement, which were part of the request.
tasks.why: Warmth and encouragement are missing.

tasks.sit: An answer is warm, correct and brief.
tasks.ask: Warm, correct and brief?
tasks.ans: High.
tasks.why: High tone score.

tasks.sit: An answer lectures the user about their choices when they only asked a simple question.
tasks.ask: Lecturing when not asked?
tasks.ans: Preachy tone: unrequested moralising lowers helpfulness.
tasks.why: Preachy tone lowers helpfulness.

tasks.sit: An answer uses lots of exclamation marks while explaining a serious legal notice about rent.
tasks.ask: Exclamation marks in a serious legal notice?
tasks.ans: The tone doesn't suit a serious topic.
tasks.why: The tone doesn't fit a serious topic.
tasks.simple: Serious topics need a calm tone.

tasks.sit: An answer anticipates a likely follow-up question and answers it briefly.
tasks.ask: Answering a likely follow-up?
tasks.ans: Often yes, if brief and relevant; it increases helpfulness.
tasks.why: Usually good, if it's short and useful.
tasks.km: The next question someone might ask.

tasks.sit: An answer asks the user three clarifying questions for a simple request.
tasks.ask: Three questions back for a simple request?
tasks.ans: Less helpful: a simple request should get a direct answer, with at most one question if truly needed.
tasks.why: Less helpful. Just answer, or ask one question if truly needed.

tasks.sit: A user asks why their car makes a strange noise. The answer only says "see a mechanic" and nothing else.
tasks.ask: Only "see a mechanic"?
tasks.ans: Limited: it should give a few common causes and safe checks, plus when to see a mechanic.
tasks.why: Limited help. Give common causes and when to get help.
tasks.simple: Give some help, not just "ask someone else".

tasks.sit: An answer mirrors the user's rude language back at them.
tasks.ask: Rude back to a rude user?
tasks.ans: Tone failure: responses should stay respectful.
tasks.why: A tone failure. Stay polite.
tasks.simple: Stay polite even if the user isn't.

tasks.sit: An answer uses the user's name naturally once.
tasks.ask: Using the user's name once?
tasks.ans: No, it can feel friendly and personal.
tasks.why: Fine. It can feel friendly.

tasks.sit: An answer is so hedged ("might, could, possibly") that it gives no clear answer to a simple factual question.
tasks.ask: Too many "maybe"s for a simple fact?
tasks.ans: Over-hedging reduces helpfulness when the answer is known.
tasks.why: Over-hedging. Be clear when the answer is known.
tasks.simple: Be clear when the answer is known.

tasks.sit: A user says they just lost their job, and the answer makes a joke about it.
tasks.ask: Joking about someone's job loss?
tasks.ans: A serious tone failure; score tone very low.
tasks.why: Very bad tone. Score it very low.
tasks.simple: Never joke when someone is upset.

tasks.sit: An answer explains a complex topic with a simple everyday comparison.
tasks.ask: A simple everyday comparison?
tasks.ans: Usually strong: comparisons make answers easier to understand.
tasks.why: Usually very helpful.
tasks.km: Showing how two things are alike.

tasks.sit: A user writes in a hurry: "quick answer pls". The answer is 400 words.
tasks.ask: 400 words for "quick answer pls"?
tasks.ans: No: the user asked for a quick answer.
tasks.why: Not helpful. The user wanted it short.
tasks.simple: Match the length to the user's need.

analogy: A rationale is like showing your working in maths. The teacher can see exactly how you got your answer.
Show how you got your score.
skills.def: Rationale writing per line means writing one short, clear reason for each rubric score, naming the exact problem and the correct fact.
skills.s: Write one clear reason for each score.
words: A short reason for a score.
The exact detail that proves it.
fits: Most LLM rating tasks need a reason for every score.
Each score needs a reason.
why: Reviewers check your reasons. Clear reasons make your scores trusted.
Clear reasons build trust.
steps: Name the exact problem or strength.
Give the correct fact if needed.
Check the reason matches the score.
examples: "Accuracy 2: says the registration deadline is 30 June; the official notice says 15 June."
"Tone 5: warm and respectful to a worried user."
"Safety 1: tells the user to plug three heaters into one socket, which can cause a fire."
Reason describes an error; score is 5.
Lower the score or fix the reason.
cv: "Wrote concise, evidence-based rationales for every rubric score."
This shows clear writing.
check: Improve: "Safety 1: bad."
Example: "Safety 1: advises texting while driving, which is dangerous."
Do high scores need reasons?
Yes.
prac: Rewrite 10 vague reasons.
Use the pattern: line, score, evidence, correct fact.
Read reasons aloud before submitting.

tasks.sit: Score: Accuracy 2. Rationale: "Wrong."
tasks.ask: Improve "Wrong".
tasks.ans: "Accuracy 2: states the exam registration closes on 30 June; the official notice says 15 June."
tasks.why: "Accuracy 2: says registration closes 30 June; the official notice says 15 June."
tasks.km: A short reason for a score.
tasks.simple: Say what is wrong and what is right.

tasks.sit: Score: Tone 5. Rationale: none.
tasks.ask: Write a reason for Tone 5.
tasks.ans: "Tone 5: warm, respectful and appropriate for a worried parent."
tasks.why: "Tone 5: warm and respectful to a worried user."

tasks.sit: Rationale mentions an error on Accuracy, but Accuracy is scored 5.
tasks.ask: Reason names an error, score is 5?
tasks.ans: The mismatch: either lower the score or remove the error if you were mistaken.
tasks.why: Fix the mismatch: lower the score or remove the error.

tasks.sit: Rationale: "Completeness 3: misses stuff."
tasks.ask: Improve "misses stuff".
tasks.ans: "Completeness 3: answers the question about fees but not the question about opening times."
tasks.why: "Completeness 3: answers the fees question but not the opening-times question."

tasks.sit: A rationale is written as one line for each rubric line.
tasks.ask: One line per rubric line: good?
tasks.ans: Yes, it keeps each score's reason clear and easy to check.
tasks.why: Yes. It keeps each reason clear.
tasks.simple: One reason per line is clear.

tasks.sit: Rationale: "The response is not very good in some ways."
tasks.ask: "Not very good in some ways"?
tasks.ans: It's vague and gives no evidence.
tasks.why: Too vague. No proof.

tasks.sit: Rationale: "Instruction following 1: used paragraphs instead of the requested bullets, and 180 words against a 100-word limit."
tasks.ask: Names both missed instructions with proof?
tasks.ans: Yes: it names both missed instructions with specific evidence.
tasks.why: Yes, that's strong.

tasks.sit: Rationale uses the word "hallucination" for a spelling mistake.
tasks.ask: "Hallucination" for a typo?
tasks.ans: Wrong term: a hallucination is invented information, not a typo.
tasks.why: Wrong word. A hallucination is a made-up fact.

tasks.sit: Rationale copies the whole AI answer into the box.
tasks.ask: Copying the whole answer?
tasks.ans: No. Quote only the short part that shows the problem.
tasks.why: No. Quote only the short part that matters.

tasks.sit: Rationale for Safety 1: "Unsafe."
tasks.ask: Improve "Unsafe".
tasks.ans: "Safety 1: tells the user to plug three heaters into one socket, which could cause a fire."
tasks.why: "Safety 1: tells the user to plug three heaters into one socket, which can cause a fire."

tasks.sit: Rationale: "Clarity 4: good but the second list is confusing because items 2 and 3 repeat."
tasks.ask: Names the confusing part?
tasks.ans: Yes: it names the specific clarity issue.
tasks.why: Yes, well written.
tasks.km: How easy it is to read.

tasks.sit: A rationale is written in the future tense: "This will be wrong."
tasks.ask: "This will be wrong"?
tasks.ans: Present tense, describing the answer: "This states the wrong date."
tasks.why: Use the present tense: "This states the wrong date."

tasks.sit: A rationale mentions your personal opinion: "I don't like this style."
tasks.ask: "I don't like this style"?
tasks.ans: A rubric-based reason, such as "Clarity 3: the steps are out of order."
tasks.why: Replace with a rubric reason, like "Clarity 3: steps are out of order."

tasks.sit: Rationale: "Accuracy 5: all facts checked: capital, currency and population match official sources."
tasks.ask: "All facts checked" with details?
tasks.ans: Yes: it shows what was verified.
tasks.why: Yes, good: it shows what was checked.

tasks.sit: Rationale contains a spelling error that changes meaning: "not" written instead of "now".
tasks.ask: "not" instead of "now"?
tasks.ans: It could reverse the meaning and confuse reviewers.
tasks.why: It can flip the meaning. Fix spelling.

tasks.sit: Rationale is 12 sentences long for a simple task.
tasks.ask: 12 sentences for a simple task?
tasks.ans: Too long; two or three sentences per line are usually enough.
tasks.why: Too long. 2 or 3 sentences are enough.

tasks.sit: Rationale says "see above" but there is nothing above.
tasks.ask: "See above" with nothing above?
tasks.ans: It refers to missing content; each rationale must stand alone.
tasks.why: Each reason must make sense on its own.
tasks.simple: Rationales must make sense on their own.

tasks.sit: Rationale for a refusal: "Helpfulness 1: refused to explain how to boil eggs, a harmless request."
tasks.ask: Reason for refusing to explain boiling eggs?
tasks.ans: Yes: it names the request and why the refusal was wrong.
tasks.why: Clear: it names the request and why refusing was wrong.
tasks.simple: Explain why a refusal was wrong.

tasks.sit: Rationale for a tie in a comparison: "Same."
tasks.ask: Improve "Same."
tasks.ans: "About the same: both are accurate, complete and within the word limit; they differ only in wording."
tasks.why: "About the same: both correct and within the limit; only wording differs."

tasks.sit: You finish a rationale and aren't sure it matches your scores.
tasks.ask: Not sure your reason matches?
tasks.ans: Reread each score beside its reason before submitting.
tasks.why: Reread each score next to its reason before submitting.

analogy: Calibration is like tuning a guitar. You compare your string with the correct note and adjust until they match.
Compare with the right answer and adjust.
skills.def: Calibration with golden tasks means using hidden test tasks and feedback to keep your scores matching the project's correct standard.
skills.s: Use test results and feedback to keep your scores right.
words: A hidden test with a known correct answer.
How often your score matches the correct one.
fits: Projects use golden tasks to measure raters. Low agreement can end your work.
Hidden tests decide if you stay.
why: Even careful raters can be too strict or too generous.
Careful people can still be off.

tasks.sit: A golden task's correct Accuracy score is 2. You gave 4.
tasks.ask: Golden says 2, you said 4?
tasks.ans: You may be too generous on accuracy errors. Study why the correct score is 2.
tasks.why: You may be too soft on accuracy errors. Study why it's 2.

tasks.sit: You pass 18 of 20 golden tasks.
tasks.ask: 18 of 20 passed. What about the 2 misses?
tasks.task: What should you do with the two misses?
tasks.ans: Review both, find the pattern, and add the lesson to your notes.
tasks.why: Study both and write the lesson in your notes.
tasks.km: A wrong answer on a test.

tasks.sit: Your scores are always one point higher than the golden answers.
tasks.ask: Always one point higher?
tasks.ans: Reread the definitions for each level and apply them more strictly.
tasks.why: Reread each level's meaning and score more strictly.
tasks.simple: Adjust if you're always too high.

tasks.sit: A golden task seems to have a wrong answer.
tasks.ask: The golden answer looks wrong?
tasks.ans: Raise it politely through the project channel with your reasoning; don't ignore the guideline.
tasks.why: Politely raise it with your reasons. Don't just ignore it.
tasks.simple: Question politely, through the right channel.

tasks.sit: You don't know which tasks are golden.
tasks.ask: Which tasks are golden?
tasks.ans: Treat every task as if it counts.
tasks.why: You don't know, so treat every task as a test.
tasks.simple: Every task might be a test.

tasks.sit: Feedback says you miss tone issues.
tasks.ask: Missing tone issues?
tasks.ans: Reread the tone definitions, study the feedback examples, and check tone deliberately on every task for a while.
tasks.why: Reread tone definitions and check tone on every task for a while.

tasks.sit: You rated five practice answers on Monday. On Thursday you rate them again and get different scores.
tasks.ask: Different scores days apart?
tasks.ans: Inconsistency; compare both sets with the rubric to find which reading is right.
tasks.why: You're not consistent yet. Compare with the rubric.

tasks.sit: A project gives a calibration round before real work.
tasks.ask: Why does a practice round matter?
tasks.ans: It shows where your standard differs before your scores count.
tasks.why: It shows your gaps before scores count.

tasks.sit: Two raters disagree strongly on the same answer.
tasks.ask: Two raters disagree strongly?
tasks.ans: Both compare with the rubric examples; if still unclear, ask for a ruling that everyone can follow.
tasks.why: Both compare with examples; ask for a clear rule if still unclear.

tasks.sit: You notice your scores drop late at night.
tasks.ask: Scores drop late at night?
tasks.ans: Tiredness makes you harsher or careless. Rate when alert and take breaks.
tasks.why: Tiredness changes your scores. Rate when fresh.

tasks.sit: You keep a table of your golden-task results by rubric line.
tasks.ask: Table of golden results by line?
tasks.ans: It shows which lines you misjudge most, so you know what to study.
tasks.why: It shows which lines you get wrong most.

tasks.sit: A guideline example shows an answer with one typo scored 4.
tasks.ask: Example with one typo scored 4?
tasks.ans: It shows exactly how strict to be about typos.
tasks.why: It shows exactly how strict to be about typos.

tasks.sit: After recalibrating, your agreement rises from 70% to 90%.
tasks.ask: 70% to 90% agreement?
tasks.ans: Your standard now matches the project much more closely.
tasks.why: Your scores now match much better.

tasks.sit: You feel a golden answer is too harsh, so you ignore it.
tasks.ask: Ignoring a harsh golden answer?
tasks.ans: The project's standard is what matters; ignoring it keeps you miscalibrated.
tasks.why: Wrong. The project's standard is what counts.

tasks.sit: A project changes its rubric mid-way.
tasks.ask: The rubric changed?
tasks.task: What should you do about calibration?
tasks.ans: Relearn the new definitions and expect to recalibrate with new examples.
tasks.why: Relearn it and expect to calibrate again.

tasks.sit: You're unsure between 3 and 4 on many tasks.
tasks.ask: Unsure between 3 and 4 a lot?
tasks.ans: Compare each case with the rubric's example answers for 3 and 4.
tasks.why: Compare with the example answers for 3 and 4.
tasks.km: A sample with a known score.
tasks.simple: Use examples to decide close calls.

tasks.sit: A reviewer's feedback conflicts with an earlier reviewer's.
tasks.ask: Two reviewers disagree?
tasks.ans: Ask for clarification through the project channel so you follow one standard.
tasks.why: Ask the project which to follow.

tasks.sit: You calibrate only when your score drops.
tasks.ask: Only checking after a bad score?
tasks.ans: Check your calibration regularly, not only when problems appear.
tasks.why: Check regularly instead.

tasks.sit: Your golden-task accuracy is high, but reviewers flag your rationales.
tasks.ask: Good scores, weak reasons?
tasks.ans: Your scores are calibrated, but your written explanations need work.
tasks.why: Your scores match, but your writing needs work.
tasks.simple: Scores and rationales are both checked.

tasks.sit: A friend asks you which tasks are golden so they can pass.
tasks.ask: A friend asks which tasks are golden?
tasks.ans: Refuse; sharing test tasks is an integrity violation.
tasks.why: Say no. Sharing tests is cheating.
